name: A Cruel Segment's Thesis
description: You are given $$$n$$$ segments on a number line. The $$$i$$$-th segment is represented as $$$[l_i, r_i]$$$. Initially, all the segments are unmarked . You perform the following operation repeatedly until there are no unmarked segments left: In the $$$k$$$-th operation, if there are at least two unmarked segments, choose any two unmarked segments $$$[l_i, r_i]$$$ and $$$[l_j, r_j]$$$, mark both of them , and add a new marked segment $$$[x_k, y_k]$$$ satisfying the following conditions: $$$l_i \leq x_k \leq r_i$$$, $$$l_j \leq y_k \leq r_j$$$, $$$x_k \leq y_k$$$. If there is exactly one unmarked segment remaining, mark it . Your task is to determine the maximum possible sum of lengths of all the marked segments at the end of the process. Note that the length of a segment $$$([l,r])$$$ is $$$r-l$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of segments. Each of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq l_i \leq r_i \leq 10^9$$$) — the $$$i$$$-th segment. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ across all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print a single integer — the maximum possible total length of all marked segments at the end of the process.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2140D — A Cruel Segment's Thesis [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
